content: Administer 1 mL of tuberculin containing 5 tuberculin units intradermally. The test result should be read 48 to 72 hours after administration. A positive result is indicated by an induration greater than 10 mm. For sensitized patients, use 1 tuberculin unit. If there is no response to 5 tuberculin units, administer 250 tuberculin units. Any suspected adverse events following vaccine administration should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Events Reporting System (VAERS) at 1-800-822-7967. Possible adverse reactions include rash, itching, vesiculation, ulceration, necrosis, pain, and hypersensitivity. A prior positive tuberculin skin test may show suppressed responsiveness within six weeks of a viral infection or inactive tuberculosis. Tuberculin contains soluble growth products derived from the tubercle bacillus. Old tuberculin (OT) is a culture filtrate of uniform potency, but purified protein derivative (PPD) is more refined and is the preferred product. Multiple puncture devices (e.g., Aplitest, SclavoTest-PPD, Tine Test-PPD) are less sensitive than intradermal administration. Several factors can reduce the ability to respond to the tuberculin test, including infections (e.g., viral infections like measles, mumps, chickenpox, HIV), live virus vaccinations (e.g., measles, mumps, rubella), bacterial infections (e.g., typhoid fever, brucellosis, typhus, leprosy, pertussis, overwhelming tuberculosis, tuberculous pleurisy), fungal infections (e.g., South American blastomycosis), certain drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents), metabolic disorders (e.g., chronic renal failure), low protein states (e.g., severe protein depletion, afibrinogenemia), age (e.g., newborns, elderly patients with waned sensitivity), stress (e.g., surgery, burns, mental illness, graft-versus-host reactions), diseases affecting lymphoid organs (e.g., Hodgkin’s disease, lymphoma, chronic leukemia, sarcoidosis), and malignancy. Any condition impairing or attenuating cell-mediated immunity, including aging, can result in a false-negative reaction. Test results are less reliable in HIV-infected individuals as CD4 counts decline. Tuberculin should not be injected subcutaneously. If this occurs, no local reaction develops, but highly sensitive individuals may experience a general febrile reaction and/or acute inflammation around old tuberculous lesions. The predictive value of the tuberculin skin test depends on the prevalence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and the relative prevalence of cross-reactions with nontuberculous mycobacteria. To prevent the transmission of infectious agents such as serum hepatitis virus, a separate, sterile, single-use disposable syringe and needle should be used for each patient. Special care must be taken to ensure the product is injected intradermally and not into a blood vessel. Before administering Aplisol, review the patient’s history for possible immediate-type hypersensitivity to the product, prior use of the agent, and any contraindications to the test. Epinephrine should be immediately available in case of an anaphylactoid or acute hypersensitivity reaction. Failure to store and handle the drug as recommended may result in a loss of potency and inaccurate test results. Reactivity to the test may be depressed or suppressed for up to 5–6 weeks following immunization with certain live viral vaccines, viral infections, or discontinuation of corticosteroids or immunosuppressive agents. Pregnancy Category C: It is not known whether the product is excreted in breast milk. Antigenic purified protein derivative (PPD) of Mycobacterium tuberculosis sensitizes patients to specific antigenic components of the organism. The onset of action for delayed hypersensitivity reactions is approximately 5–6 hours, with a peak effect occurring at 48–72 hours.
